title: Quantum Machine Learning in Medical Imaging: A Primer for Radiologists
authors: Ruben Ortiz Cordero, Gaven K. Smart, Harshada Gothankar, Emilio Supsupin, Priya Bhosale, Mayur Virarkar
abstract: Deep learning has transformed radiology, but the computational cost of training and deploying modern models is outpacing what classical hardware can support. Quantum computing has been proposed as one response to this bottleneck: an n-qubit system can represent $2^n$ states simultaneously, although practical speedups require efficient algorithms, data encoding, and measurement strategies rather than superposition alone. This review introduces radiologists to five core quantum concepts, qubits, superposition, entanglement, quantum gates, and quantum circuits, and to the superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic hardware platforms that define the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era. We then summarize the quantum machine learning architectures most often applied to medical imaging (quantum support vector machines, quantum neural networks, variational quantum circuits, and quantum convolutional neural networks) and quantum image representations such as the flexible representation of quantum images (FRQI) and the novel enhanced quantum representation (NEQR). Reported applications include brain tumor classification and segmentation on MRI, pneumonia detection on chest radiographs, skin and breast lesion classification, CT and PET reconstruction, and ultrasound denoising. Nearly all published systems are hybrid quantum-classical pipelines evaluated on small, downsampled benchmark datasets or simulators, and clinical deployment is not yet feasible. We conclude with current limitations and translational priorities for radiology.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum machine learning offers experimental approaches to medical imaging, but this review finds that clinical deployment is not yet feasible.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Practical value depends on efficient data encoding, quantum algorithms, measurement strategies, and integration with classical imaging pipelines—not superposition alone.
method: Introduces core quantum concepts and superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic hardware.
Reviews quantum support vector machines, neural networks, variational circuits, and convolutional networks.
Surveys FRQI and NEQR image representations and medical imaging applications.
infographic.evidence_signal: Nearly all reported systems use hybrid quantum-classical pipelines evaluated on small, downsampled benchmark datasets or simulators.
infographic.watch_item: Results on simplified datasets or simulators do not establish a practical quantum advantage for clinical imaging.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Machine Learning in Medical Imaging: A Primer for Radiologists

title: Classical Pre-Training of Large Shallow Parametrized Quantum Circuits through Pauli Propagation and deployment on Quantum Hardware
authors: Saverio Monaco, Jamal Slim, Ran Xue, Dirk Krücker, Kerstin Borras
abstract: Scaling parametrized quantum circuits to a larger number of qubits is a central challenge in Quantum Machine Learning: gradient estimation via the parameter-shift rule quickly becomes prohibitively expensive, while gradient-free optimizers offer limited convergence guarantees. We apply the Pauli propagation framework to a broad class of Quantum Machine Learning problems in which the loss is expressed as a function of expectation values of the circuit's observables, while keeping the relevant quantity of interest, such as the quantum state or its samples, classically intractable to compute. By propagating the observables backward through the circuit, we obtain an explicit parametric expression for the loss that can be minimized entirely on classical hardware. We also present complementary strategies to make propagation tractable at large scale, including weight-based and degree-based truncations and pruning heuristics. We demonstrate the approach on two benchmarks run on 64-qubit circuits: Variational Quantum Eigensolver on a two-dimensional Ising model, and training of a discrete-type generative model for binary images. In both cases, the classically pre-trained parameters are deployed on the IBM quantum processor ibm_berlin. For generative learning, we additionally show that the circuits considered here require substantially fewer parametrized gates than IQP-style ansätze, reducing transpilation overhead and making deployment on current quantum hardware feasible.

infographic.key_insight: Pauli propagation enables classical pre-training of large, shallow parametrized quantum circuits while leaving target quantum states or samples classically intractable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Moving loss optimization to classical hardware reduces reliance on costly quantum gradient estimation before deploying trained circuits on quantum processors.
method: Propagate observables backward through the circuit to derive an explicit parameter-dependent loss.
Use weight- and degree-based truncation plus pruning heuristics to control propagation cost.
Optimize parameters classically, then deploy the trained circuits on quantum hardware.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports two 64-qubit benchmarks—VQE for a two-dimensional Ising model and binary-image generative learning—with trained parameters deployed on IBM's ibm_berlin processor.
infographic.watch_item: Truncation and pruning make propagation tractable but can introduce approximation error that requires validation for each circuit and task.
infographic.paper_title: Classical Pre-Training of Large Shallow Parametrized Quantum Circuits through Pauli Propagation and deployment on Quantum Hardware

title: Distributed Quantum-Centric Supercomputing with Multi-Layered Generative Learning for Intermolecular Interactions
authors: Chayan Patra, Prayas Ghosh, Adwait Patkhedkar, Rahul Maitra
abstract: Quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) approaches, such as sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), combine quantum processors with high-performance computers (HPC), offering a promising route toward solving challenging electronic structure problems. However, implementation of QCSC approaches to large active space calculations is constrained by the associated number of qubits, deep quantum circuits, sampling cost, and large-scale Hamiltonian diagonalization. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a distributed QCSC framework that decomposes complex molecular problems into parallel sub-problems requiring fewer qubits, shallower circuits, and reduced shot budgets. A physically motivated, two-step aggregation scheme then reconstructs the global solution: first, a computational bit assignment strategy optimizes a cost function to appropriately map local bit indices to global ones, yielding a mapped tensor product state (MTPS); second, an inter-fragment correlation recovery module restores missing cross-fragment interactions. Herein, we employ a multi-layered generative machine learning architecture, starting with utilizing the recently proposed physics-informed generative SQD (PIGen-SQD) as a distributed QCSC solver, followed by a secondary generative module to model configuration distributions and identify dominant sectors of the global Hilbert space. For water and formamide dimers, our method achieves up to $95\%$ reduction in the diagonalization dimension while enhancing energy accuracy by an order of magnitude over conventional SQD. Furthermore, application to the water hexamer ($\mathrm{(H_2O)_6}$) cage successfully decomposes a 120-qubit problem into six 20-qubit monomeric subsystems, and stitches the monomers under a dimeric approximation, demonstrating excellent agreement with the reference classical methods.

infographic.key_insight: Distributed quantum-centric supercomputing combines fragment-level quantum calculations with generative learning to reconstruct molecular interactions using smaller computational subproblems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets lower qubit counts, shallower circuits, reduced sampling costs, and smaller classical diagonalizations for electronic-structure calculations.
method: Solve molecular fragments in parallel using physics-informed generative sample-based quantum diagonalization (PIGen-SQD).
Optimize local-to-global bit assignments to assemble a mapped tensor product state.
Use a second generative module to identify dominant global configurations and recover inter-fragment correlations.
infographic.evidence_signal: For water and formamide dimers, the abstract reports up to 95% smaller diagonalization dimensions and an order-of-magnitude improvement in energy accuracy over conventional SQD; a 120-qubit water hexamer problem was split into six 20-qubit subsystems with excellent agreement with classical references.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to the reported molecular systems, and the hexamer uses a dimeric approximation whose accuracy for stronger many-body correlations remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Distributed Quantum-Centric Supercomputing with Multi-Layered Generative Learning for Intermolecular Interactions

title: Automating quantum circuit optimization with AI agents
authors: Marcos Crichigno, Steve Flammia
abstract: Compiling quantum algorithms for real devices involves hard optimization problems that can decide whether an algorithm runs at scale. We present a general method for solving such problems with AI agents, with every result certified. It builds on autoresearch loops, in which agents iteratively improve programs against a fixed evaluator and which have recently improved quantum cryptanalysis circuits, and adds two elements: a frozen, exact verifier certifies every result, and this verifier, together with the challenge around it, is built by an agent that formulates the problem with a researcher and validates the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results before any solution exists. The method applies to any optimization problem whose solutions can be verified exactly and efficiently. We apply it to three compilation problems in quantum simulation, namely fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis. In each, the agents improved substantially on published or standard constructions, reducing the cost being optimized by up to 73% at the largest sizes tested and outperforming a state-of-the-art optimizer for fermion-to-qubit encodings. Every submission is a program accompanied by its agent's notes, so the ideas behind each improvement are recorded in human-readable form; later agents built on them, and we describe them here. These results open the way to automated, certified discovery across quantum circuit design and beyond.

infographic.key_insight: AI agents improved quantum compilation constructions through iterative program optimization, with every result certified by a frozen, exact verifier.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could lower quantum circuit implementation costs while making automated optimization results independently checkable.
method: An agent formulates the optimization challenge with a researcher and builds an exact verifier.
Validate the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results, then freeze it.
Run iterative agent optimization, retaining programs and human-readable notes for later agents to build on.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis, agents reduced the targeted cost by up to 73% at the largest sizes tested and outperformed a state-of-the-art fermion-to-qubit encoding optimizer.
infographic.watch_item: Exact certification depends on verifier correctness, and reductions in the optimized cost do not by themselves establish equivalent gains on quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Automating quantum circuit optimization with AI agents

title: Resource Analysis of Quantum Optimization Algorithms via Variational Methods
authors: Vitor Dallabona, Lucas Friedrich, Jonas Maziero
abstract: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are promising approaches for solving combinatorial optimization problems on near-term quantum devices. However, the role played by quantum resources such as entanglement and coherence during the optimization process remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate the evolution of these resources in two VQAs--the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and the Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON)--applied to the Minimum Vertex Cover problem. We employ a variational resource-quantification framework based on the Bures metric and Uhlmann's theorem, in which an auxiliary quantum circuit is optimized to identify the closest resource-free states. This approach allows us to quantify Bures entanglement and Bures coherence of the algorithmic states without requiring full quantum state tomography. For the considered problem instance, QAOA exhibits a pronounced accumulation of entanglement in its initial layers, followed by a progressive reduction as the algorithm converges toward the optimal solution. Its coherence likewise decreases overall with increasing circuit depth, although a finite residual value persists due to the degeneracy of the optimal-solution subspace. In contrast, FALQON exhibits a substantially lower entanglement peak, reached at larger circuit depth, followed by a decay as convergence proceeds. Its coherence decreases smoothly and monotonically together with the optimization error. These results reveal distinct quantum-resource trajectories associated with the two optimization strategies and illustrate how entanglement and coherence evolve as variational quantum states approach solutions of a classical combinatorial optimization problem.

infographic.key_insight: QAOA and FALQON follow distinct entanglement and coherence trajectories as they approach Minimum Vertex Cover solutions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tracking these resources without full state tomography could help characterize quantum optimization circuits for near-term devices.
method: Apply QAOA and FALQON to Minimum Vertex Cover.
Optimize auxiliary circuits to identify closest resource-free states.
Quantify Bures entanglement and coherence using Uhlmann’s theorem.
infographic.evidence_signal: For the considered instance, QAOA shows an early entanglement peak and residual coherence, while FALQON shows a lower, later entanglement peak and smoothly decreasing coherence.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern one problem instance; broader generalization and auxiliary-circuit optimization costs remain to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: Resource Analysis of Quantum Optimization Algorithms via Variational Methods

title: Quantum Fokker-Planck solvers as trainable generative models
authors: Tariq Mahassen, Marcin Jastrzebski, Oleksandr Kyriienko
abstract: We develop and analyze generative models based on quantum solvers of stochastic differential equations. Unlike the common approach based on layered variational quantum circuits with parameterized rotations, we parameterize the potential of a Langevin process. The associated Fokker-Planck (FP) equations are Hermitianized and solved using a linear combination of cosine operators implemented through quantum singular value transformation. By encoding the square root of the stationary density, the model enables sampling through computational-basis measurements and is efficiently controlled by coefficients of the block-encoded diagonal potential. We train the proposed model to match empirical distributions within the family described by FP equations, demonstrating parameter recovery for multivariate probability distributions. Crucially, the model remains trainable at scale. Sample-efficient and convex optimization for in-distribution targets arises from a physics-informed inductive bias and holds regardless of the dimensionality of the problem. We provide circuit constructions and efficient block encodings of the main components of the algorithm and analyze resource requirements. Our approach frames quantum generative learning as quantum model discovery and provides a foundation for extending this framework to high-dimensional, strongly correlated scientific data.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum generative models can learn a Langevin potential instead of circuit rotations, using Fokker–Planck solvers to encode and sample its stationary distribution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This physics-informed approach offers a route to trainable quantum models for scientific distributions, with efficient block encodings and analyzed circuit resources.
method: Parameterize the potential governing a Langevin process.
Hermitianize the Fokker–Planck equation and solve it using cosine operators implemented through quantum singular value transformation.
Encode the square root of the stationary density and sample via computational-basis measurements.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports parameter recovery for multivariate distributions and sample-efficient, convex optimization for in-distribution targets, independent of problem dimensionality.
infographic.watch_item: The stated optimization guarantees concern in-distribution targets; performance on strongly correlated scientific data and practical hardware remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Fokker-Planck solvers as trainable generative models

title: Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (MQE): A Selective State Space Model for Scalable Ground State Simulations in Quantum Chemistry
authors: G. X. A. Petronilo, M. R. Araújo, Erico S. Teixeira, Clebson Cruz
abstract: Predicting molecular electronic structure using Quantum Computing approaches is a challenge in Computational Chemistry. Traditional Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) are typically hindered by optimization challenges. The alternative Generative Quantum Eigensolver (GQE) mitigates this by reformulating ground-state search as discrete sequence generation, but its Transformer backbone suffers from quadratic computational complexity, bottlenecking scalability for larger molecules. To address this, we introduce the Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (Mamba-QE), which replaces the Transformer with a Selective State Space Model (SSM) to process operator sequences with linear $\mathcal{O}(L)$ complexity. Additionally, we integrate a distance-conditioned mechanism enabling the direct prediction of complete potential energy surfaces (PES). Evaluated on the $H_2$ molecule, Mamba-QE reproduces Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) reference energies well within chemical accuracy, achieving an energy error below $3\times10^{-6}$ Ha across 16 geometries with zero variational violations. Mamba-QE maintains high expressive power while establishing a robust, scalable foundation for quantum simulations of complex molecular systems.

infographic.key_insight: Mamba-QE replaces the Transformer in a Generative Quantum Eigensolver with a selective state space model, enabling linear-complexity operator-sequence processing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture targets sequence-processing bottlenecks in molecular ground-state simulation, with distance conditioning supporting potential energy surface prediction.
method: Frame ground-state search as discrete quantum-operator sequence generation.
Use a selective state space model with O(L) sequence-processing complexity.
Condition generation on molecular distance to predict potential energy surfaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: On H₂ across 16 geometries, the abstract reports energy errors below 3×10⁻⁶ Ha relative to Full Configuration Interaction, with zero variational violations.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation is limited to H₂; linear sequence-processing complexity does not establish end-to-end scalability for larger molecules.
infographic.paper_title: Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (MQE): A Selective State Space Model for Scalable Ground State Simulations in Quantum Chemistry

title: Low-frustration block encodings by patch routing
authors: Minzhao Liu, Abeynaya Gnanasekaran, Ananth Kaushik, Siddharth Hariprakash, Alireza Marefat Khah, Martin Roetteler
abstract: Block-encoding has emerged as a core primitive in many quantum algorithms, including quantum simulation. In this work, we design efficient and extensible methods for generating low-frustration block encodings of frustrated lattice Hamiltonians built from repeated local interaction patches through a technique we call "patch routing". We construct block encodings for a full Hamiltonian by first block-encoding a small local patch and then using a SWAP-style routing network to coherently apply the local patch encoding across the lattice. The expensive, local block-encoding cost is paid only once per query and is independent of lattice size, whereas the comparatively inexpensive routing network grows linearly with the lattice size, dominating at large sizes. Our method allows for a hierarchical structure in which larger patches can be block-encoded with small normalization factors, albeit at a higher (local, non-extensive) block-encoding cost, thereby reducing overall query complexity in an algorithm. We exploit symmetries and algebraic structures in local interactions to construct efficient block encodings, and we apply these techniques to the Heisenberg, Fermi-Hubbard, and honeycomb spin-liquid models. For a $120\times 120$ square-lattice $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model near maximal frustration ($J_2/J_1=0.4-0.6$), our methods result in a $15-17\times$ reduction in the leading $T$ cost per qubitized-QPE run (ignoring initial state preparation and overlap) relative to prior state-of-the-art Pauli LCU constructions. Corresponding reductions are approximately $3\times$ for the $120\times120$ Fermi-Hubbard model at half-filling. For time evolution of the honeycomb spin-liquid model on $120\times120$ unit cells, the leading cost is reduced by $5\times$. Our framework provides a systematic way forward for larger and more accurate fault-tolerant simulations of real-world quantum systems.

infographic.key_insight: Patch routing builds low-frustration block encodings of lattice Hamiltonians by reusing one local patch encoding through coherent SWAP-style routing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can reduce fault-tolerant quantum simulation costs by separating lattice-independent local encoding work from routing that scales linearly with lattice size.
method: Block-encode a small interaction patch using local symmetries and algebraic structure.
Coherently route the patch encoding across the lattice with a SWAP-style network.
Use larger hierarchical patches to trade higher local encoding cost for lower normalization and query complexity.
infographic.evidence_signal: For 120×120 systems, the abstract reports leading-cost reductions of 15–17× for frustrated J1–J2 Heisenberg qubitized QPE, approximately 3× for half-filled Fermi–Hubbard QPE, and 5× for honeycomb spin-liquid time evolution.
infographic.watch_item: Reported QPE savings exclude initial state preparation and overlap, while routing dominates costs at large lattice sizes.
infographic.paper_title: Low-frustration block encodings by patch routing

title: Digital Quantum Simulation of Dynamics in Interacting Fields
authors: Zhiyao Li
abstract: Matter under extreme conditions behaves as a non-equilibrium, strongly-interacting quantum system. Such systems are in the non-perturbative regime of quantum chromodynamics (QCD), where their time evolution is classically intractable. Quantum computing offers a promising alternative, but present-day devices are limited in qubit count and circuit depth, so efficient formulations and algorithms are key to scaling toward experimentally relevant QCD simulations. A scalable framework is established for simulating energy loss and hadronization in 1+1-dimensional SU(2) lattice gauge theory, in which a heavy quark traverses a lattice of light quarks. Classical lattice QCD methods are translated into physics-informed circuits to prepare the interacting ground state. The evolution is run on IBM's quantum processor ibm_pittsburgh, where the charge distribution and energy loss are measured. A further study develops the quantum simulation of the fully gauge-fixed SU(2) Hamiltonian in a mixed basis, a formulation that is expected to remain efficient at all gauge couplings. Digitizing the continuous gauge fields with as few as three qubits per plaquette reproduces low-energy observables with $10^{-3}$ precision. Scaling to larger systems is limited by resource overhead, which motivates truncations that preserve the relevant observables. Sequency Hierarchy Truncation (SeqHT) exploits the hierarchy in basis-operator contributions. Demonstrated on the adiabatic preparation of the $λφ^4$ ground state on ibm_sherbrooke, SeqHT reduces circuit depth by ~30%, suppressing hardware noise in the extracted observables. All simulations in this dissertation are validated on quantum hardware against classical benchmarks. These studies advance quantum simulations of real-time QCD dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-informed circuits, compact gauge-field encodings, and operator truncation advance resource-efficient quantum simulation of interacting-field dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These methods reduce qubit and circuit-depth demands on a path toward real-time QCD simulations beyond classical reach.
method: Prepare interacting ground states and simulate heavy-quark energy loss in 1+1D SU(2) lattice gauge theory.
Digitize a fully gauge-fixed SU(2) Hamiltonian in a mixed basis.
Apply Sequency Hierarchy Truncation (SeqHT) to reduce ground-state preparation depth.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports quantum-hardware validation against classical benchmarks, low-energy observables reproduced to 10⁻³ precision with three qubits per plaquette, and approximately 30% circuit-depth reduction with SeqHT.
infographic.watch_item: Larger systems remain resource-limited, and truncations must preserve the observables relevant to each simulation.
infographic.paper_title: Digital Quantum Simulation of Dynamics in Interacting Fields

title: Robustness of Quantum Correlations and Controlled Teleportation Fidelity under Noisy Channels
authors: S. Archana, Aditi Das, Venkat Abhignan, R. Muthuganesan
abstract: In distributed quantum computing, quantum networks provide a potential infrastructure for long-range quantum information processing. Controlled quantum teleportation (CQT) is a key practically relevant protocol that can connect two parties on a network and enables a third party, the controller to allow or abort the secure teleportation of an arbitrary single-qubit state between the two parties. We investigate the robustness of a three-qubit GHZ resource under bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping noise. Using the Kraus-operator formalism, we characterize the noisy resource through multipartite quantum discord, genuine multipartite concurrence (GMC), localizable entanglement (LE), and CQT fidelity. We also outline a proof-of-concept photonic implementation for preparing the three-qubit GHZ resource and realizing the CQT protocol, which could enable experimental investigation of the effects of noise. Our results show that bit-flip and amplitude-damping noise generally preserve useful mutipartite quantum correlations over broader noise parameter ranges. Interestingly, multipartite discord exhibits freezing under bit-flip noise over a finite parameter regime. Moreover, discord can persist beyond the sudden death of genuine multipartite entanglement, revealing the distinct robustness of nonclassical correlations. We further demonstrate that CQT fidelity which characterizes the performance of CQT can exceed the classical threshold even after GMC vanishes, while LE more closely reflects the operational usefulness of the noisy resource. These findings highlight the complementary roles of quantum correlations and entanglement in assessing the resilience of GHZ-based protocols.

infographic.key_insight: Noisy GHZ resources can retain nonclassical correlations and controlled teleportation fidelity above the classical threshold even after genuine multipartite entanglement vanishes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Localizable entanglement may better indicate the operational usefulness of noisy GHZ resources for controlled teleportation in distributed quantum networks.
method: Model bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping noise using Kraus operators.
Evaluate multipartite discord, genuine multipartite concurrence, localizable entanglement, and controlled teleportation fidelity.
Outline a proof-of-concept photonic GHZ preparation and teleportation implementation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The analysis finds broader correlation robustness under bit-flip and amplitude-damping noise, finite-regime discord freezing under bit-flip noise, and above-classical teleportation fidelity after genuine multipartite concurrence vanishes.
infographic.watch_item: The photonic implementation is proposed rather than experimentally demonstrated in the abstract, so hardware-level robustness remains unverified.
infographic.paper_title: Robustness of Quantum Correlations and Controlled Teleportation Fidelity under Noisy Channels

title: Fidelity Dynamics of a Jaynes--Cummings Qubit under Markovian and Non-Markovian Coupling Noise
authors: Fang Wang, Da-Wei Luo, Ting Yu
abstract: We analytically investigate the fidelity dynamics of a Jaynes--Cummings qubit coupled to a single-mode cavity in the presence of stochastic fluctuations of the qubit--cavity coupling. Such fluctuations naturally arise in cavity- and circuit-QED platforms due to fabrication imperfections, control-field noise, mechanical vibrations, and environmental disturbances. Since the qubit--cavity coupling governs the rate of coherent energy and information exchange, understanding the effects of its fluctuations is essential for assessing the performance of quantum communication, quantum sensing, and quantum information-processing protocols. We consider both Gaussian white noise and Ornstein--Uhlenbeck noise with finite correlation time as models for the coupling fluctuations. Exploiting the closed dynamics within each excitation manifold, we derive exact analytical expressions for the noise-averaged density matrix and the fidelity relative to the ideal noiseless evolution. We show that the fidelity is determined by a single decoherence factor governed by the integrated noise correlation function, establishing a direct connection between microscopic coupling fluctuations and macroscopic coherence loss. In the white-noise limit, the fidelity decays exponentially, whereas finite noise correlation times produce nonexponential decay and slower coherence loss. We further show that the crossover between Markovian-like and non-Markovian regimes is controlled by the ratio of the noise correlation rate to the coherent coupling strength, and that decoherence increases with photon number because of the enhanced effective qubit--cavity coupling. These results provide a unified analytical framework for quantifying decoherence induced by stochastic coupling fluctuations and for evaluating the robustness of cavity-QED protocols under correlated noise.

infographic.key_insight: Exact analysis links Jaynes–Cummings qubit fidelity to integrated coupling-noise correlations, with finite correlation times producing nonexponential decay and slower coherence loss than white noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps assess the robustness of cavity- and circuit-QED protocols against fluctuating qubit–cavity coupling, including stronger decoherence at higher photon numbers.
method: Model coupling fluctuations using Gaussian white noise and finite-memory Ornstein–Uhlenbeck noise.
Exploit closed dynamics within each excitation manifold to derive exact noise-averaged density matrices and fidelities.
Express fidelity through a single decoherence factor governed by integrated noise correlations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports exact analytical results comparing noise models and identifying a crossover controlled by the noise correlation rate relative to coherent coupling strength; no experimental validation is described.
infographic.watch_item: Device-level predictions require checking whether the assumed noise models and single-mode dynamics capture the hardware’s dominant noise and loss channels.
infographic.paper_title: Fidelity Dynamics of a Jaynes--Cummings Qubit under Markovian and Non-Markovian Coupling Noise

title: Exploiting the Weyl-Chamber Structure for Hardware-Aware Quantum Circuit Compression
authors: Neel Misciasci, Isabel Nha Minh Le, Christian B. Mendl
abstract: Quantum circuit compression based on tensor networks enables long-time simulation of quantum many-body dynamics on near-term hardware. While Riemannian optimization has been successfully employed for this purpose, it typically optimizes over the manifold of generic two-qubit unitaries. Consequently, the resulting gates must still be synthesized into the hardware's native gate set via KAK decomposition, an overhead that partially negates the original compression gain. We show that Riemannian-optimized gates already exhibit a predictable Weyl structure: near-$R_{ZZ}$ for the Ising model and near-fSim for the Heisenberg XXZ model. Building on this insight, we investigate whether parameterized optimization directly over the native gate set can offer a beneficial trade-off between expressivity and circuit efficiency by reducing the circuit's dimensionality. When comparing the two approaches, we find that the small residual Weyl parameters neglected by the latter are essential for high compression of the Ising propagator, whereas for the Heisenberg propagator, the native XXZ structure can be exploited directly to build a more efficient compressed circuit.

infographic.key_insight: Optimized two-qubit gates exhibit model-specific Weyl structure, but restricting gates to native forms improves compression efficiency for Heisenberg XXZ dynamics, not Ising dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hardware-aware gate optimization can reduce synthesis overhead, provided native-gate restrictions preserve the expressivity needed for accurate compression.
method: Compress many-body time-evolution circuits using tensor networks and Riemannian optimization.
Analyze optimized gates in the Weyl chamber: near-RZZ for Ising and near-fSim for Heisenberg XXZ.
Compare generic two-qubit optimization with parameterized optimization over native gate sets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that small residual Weyl parameters are essential for high Ising compression, while exploiting native XXZ structure yields a more efficient compressed Heisenberg circuit.
infographic.watch_item: Near-native gate structure alone does not justify discarding small Weyl parameters; the compression impact must be checked for each model.
infographic.paper_title: Exploiting the Weyl-Chamber Structure for Hardware-Aware Quantum Circuit Compression

title: Demonstrating RFSoC-based Control of a Fully Connected Exchange-Only Qubit
authors: Abigail L. Wessels, M. Garrett Bimstefer, Joseph D. Broz, Alen Senanian, Andrew E. Oriani
abstract: Semiconductor triple-quantum dots (TQDs) are a promising platform for scalable quantum information processing, but the community has so far lacked access to affordable and flexible high-speed control electronics. SpinQICK, an open-source spin qubit-control package built on the Xilinx Radio Frequency System-on-Chip (RFSoC), directly addresses this gap by leveraging the high sampling-rate signal generation and advanced digital signal processing (DSP) capabilities of the Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit (QICK) to enable precise time-domain voltage control and readout of semiconductor spin qubits. In this paper, we use spinQICK to demonstrate coherent control, state preparation, and readout of a fully connected triangular exchange-only device. We also introduce and experimentally verify a novel dynamical decoupling (DD) sequence enabled by the triangular TQD and leverage its unique decoupling properties to characterize electrical noise. These results establish spinQICK as a low-cost, flexible platform for semiconductor spin qubit control and provide a pathway for hardware optimization through qubit-level noise diagnostics.

infographic.key_insight: SpinQICK enables RFSoC-based control of a fully connected triangular exchange-only qubit, including coherent manipulation, state preparation, and readout.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The open-source platform offers a low-cost, flexible route to semiconductor spin-qubit control and hardware optimization through qubit-level noise diagnostics.
method: Build on QICK and Xilinx RFSoC signal generation and digital signal processing.
Apply precise time-domain voltage control to a triangular triple-quantum-dot device.
Implement a geometry-enabled dynamical decoupling sequence to characterize electrical noise.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experimental demonstrations of coherent control, state preparation, and readout, plus verification of the new dynamical decoupling sequence, but provides no numerical performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability and quantitative control fidelity are not established by the abstract; the demonstrated decoupling sequence relies on triangular device connectivity.
infographic.paper_title: Demonstrating RFSoC-based Control of a Fully Connected Exchange-Only Qubit

title: Symmetry-Preserving and Scalable Variational Circuits for the Lattice Gross-Neveu Model
authors: Vivan Bhatt, Zhongtian Dong, Kyoungchul Kong, Kwangmin Yu
abstract: We study variational preparation of ground states and sector-resolved excited states in the $(1+1)$-dimensional lattice Gross-Neveu model. We construct fixed circuits preserving either total fermion number or every flavor number, and a problem-specific scalable-circuit adaptive variational quantum eigensolver (SC-ADAPT-VQE). Classical circuit benchmarks cover massless and massive systems through 30 qubits, using exact-diagonalization and tensor-network reference results. Imposing flavor-number conservation improves the achieved energies in the completed two-flavor comparisons. Selected massive fixed-ansatz benchmarks with one to four flavors have relative energy errors of approximately $1 \times 10^{-5}$ - $2 \times 10^{-4}$, smaller than the quoted literature errors where available, although discretizations and computational resources differ. The adaptive pool combines translated bulk and boundary-sensitive generators with an interaction-sensitive cross-flavor family. Selected massive SC-ADAPT benchmarks with one to three flavors have relative energy errors below $2.1 \times 10^{-3}$. For one flavor, matrix-product-state evaluations extend the transferred circuits to 60-400 qubits without target-side operator selection or parameter optimization, giving energy deviations of approximately $0.35\%$ - $1.76\%$ from density-matrix renormalization-group reference values at maximum bond dimension 256. At fixed flavor number, range caps, and append count, the adaptive construction has a precompilation local-factor count linear in volume and a volume-independent shared-parameter count; fixed-accuracy performance at arbitrary volumes remains unestablished. Sequential deflation also prepares low-lying states within a fixed flavor-number sector, with projector fidelities providing a basis-independent assessment of degenerate target eigenspaces.

infographic.key_insight: Symmetry-preserving variational circuits achieve accurate lattice Gross–Neveu energies, while transferred adaptive circuits extend one-flavor evaluations to 400 qubits without target-side optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: At fixed flavor number, range caps, and append count, the adaptive construction offers linear precompilation local-factor scaling with volume and a volume-independent shared-parameter count.
method: Build fixed circuits conserving total fermion number or each flavor number.
Use SC-ADAPT-VQE with bulk, boundary-sensitive, and cross-flavor generators.
Prepare sector-resolved excited states by sequential deflation and assess degenerate eigenspaces using projector fidelities.
infographic.evidence_signal: Classical benchmarks through 30 qubits report selected massive fixed-circuit relative energy errors of approximately 10⁻⁵–2×10⁻⁴; one-flavor MPS evaluations at 60–400 qubits show approximately 0.35%–1.76% deviations from DMRG references.
infographic.watch_item: Fixed-accuracy scaling to arbitrary volumes remains unestablished, and the reported benchmarks are classical circuit evaluations rather than quantum-hardware demonstrations.
infographic.paper_title: Symmetry-Preserving and Scalable Variational Circuits for the Lattice Gross-Neveu Model

title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence
authors: Chia-Hsien Huang, Hsi-Sheng Goan
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum gates that combine short duration, high fidelity, and robustness to noise. As quantum processors scale, robustness becomes increasingly important because exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration of individual gates become impractical. We present a comprehensive optimal-control framework for controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons that systematically accounts for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms, including energy relaxation and dephasing. Using smooth, single-shot flux pulses, we obtain 12-ns CZ gates---close to the theoretical speed limit of 11.6 ns---with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2\times10^{-5}$ level. We construct dephasing noise models, calibrated against published experimental measurements, that capture fast dephasing from room-temperature control electronics and slow dephasing from $1/f$ flux noise. Using these models, we identify dephasing sweet spots that suppress sensitivity to dephasing noise. We further exploit transmon asymmetry as a design parameter to access distinct noise-resilient operating regimes. These results establish an experimentally applicable framework for balancing gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.

infographic.key_insight: Optimized flux pulses enable 12-ns transmon CZ gates with intrinsic errors near 2×10⁻⁵, while identifying operating regimes resilient to dephasing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps balance gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness, potentially reducing characterization and recalibration overhead in scalable superconducting processors.
method: Optimize smooth, single-shot flux pulses for directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons.
Model intrinsic Hamiltonian errors, energy relaxation, and fast and slow dephasing.
Identify dephasing sweet spots and exploit transmon asymmetry for noise resilience.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 12-ns gates near an 11.6-ns theoretical speed limit and intrinsic errors around 2×10⁻⁵, using dephasing models calibrated against published experimental measurements.
infographic.watch_item: The reported intrinsic error excludes decoherence contributions, and the abstract does not report experimental validation of the optimized gates.
infographic.paper_title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence

title: Hardware-Friendly Estimation of LCU-Based Expectation Values via Quantum-to-Classical Workload Shifting
authors: Hari Hara Suthan Chittoor, Thirumalai Manimaran
abstract: Estimating the expectation value of an observable $O$ for a quantum state evolved under a general, possibly non-unitary, operator $A$ is a fundamental task in quantum simulation, chemistry, and variational algorithms. Existing linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) approaches implement $A$ on hardware, requiring ancilla qubits, controlled unitaries and, in randomized variants, fresh circuit executions for every Monte Carlo sample. These costs are prohibitive on NISQ and early fault-tolerant devices. We propose HERMES (Hardware-Efficient Reusable Measurements for Estimating LCU-based expectation valueS), which moves the processing of $A$ entirely to the classical domain. Expanding $A$ and $O$ in the Pauli basis and sampling pairs of Pauli terms classically, HERMES rewrites $μ= \mathrm{Tr}(OAρA^{\dagger})/\mathrm{Tr}(AρA^{\dagger})$ as a ratio of weighted sums of Pauli expectation values on the unmodified state $ρ$, with no ancillas, controlled unitaries, or quantum implementation of $A$. A two-level measurement reduction scheme (Pauli deduplication and commuting-group partitioning) bounds the number of distinct measurement settings independently of the sample count, unlike randomized LCU methods whose circuit executions grow linearly with it. On ground-state energy estimation of $\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{LiH}$ via imaginary-time evolution, HERMES matches or beats Pauli single-ancilla LCU baseline using shallow circuits with no two-qubit gates beyond state preparation under qubit-wise commuting grouping. It is also more robust to noise and completes a noisy $\mathrm{LiH}$ simulation infeasible for the baseline, at the cost of classical overhead growing with the number of Pauli terms in $A$.

infographic.key_insight: HERMES shifts LCU operator processing to classical computation, estimating transformed-state expectation values from reusable measurements of the original quantum state.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It eliminates ancillas, controlled unitaries, and quantum implementation of the transformation operator, reducing hardware demands on NISQ and early fault-tolerant devices.
method: Expand the transformation operator and observable in the Pauli basis, then sample Pauli-term pairs classically.
Compute the target expectation as a ratio of weighted sums of Pauli measurements on the unmodified state.
Deduplicate Pauli terms and group commuting measurements to bound distinct measurement settings independently of classical sample count.
infographic.evidence_signal: In H₂ and LiH imaginary-time ground-state energy evaluations, HERMES matched or outperformed a Pauli single-ancilla LCU baseline, showed greater noise robustness, and completed a noisy LiH simulation infeasible for that baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Classical overhead grows with the number of Pauli terms in the transformation operator; bounded measurement settings do not imply bounded total measurement shots.
infographic.paper_title: Hardware-Friendly Estimation of LCU-Based Expectation Values via Quantum-to-Classical Workload Shifting

title: Modular optical fault-tolerant quantum computation via an interface between verified resources and online logical operations
authors: Kosuke Fukui, Takaya Matsuura, Yohji Chin, Shohei Kiryu, Takaya Hoshi, Kan Takase
abstract: We introduce a factory--processor interface architecture for modular optical fault-tolerant quantum computation that separates code-dependent encoded-resource preparation from reusable online logical processing on a common Gaussian optical processor. Beyond encoded resources, the interface specifies logical outputs, code-to-mode mapping, measurement roles, frame updates, verification records, and resource-injection boundaries. As a concrete realization, we combine an offline verified Bell-resource factory based on a recursively concatenated $C_4$ code with physical Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP) qubits with an online time-domain measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) processor. Under the specified additive-displacement-noise model and fixed postselection policy, simulations support the finite-level logical Bell-error ordering $P_5<P_4<P_3<P_2$ at 12.25 dB of effective GKP displacement-noise quality, both with and without the prescribed additional post-injection displacement noise. At 15.6 dB and $L=2$, a separate fixed-sample evaluation gives one-sided 95$\%$ Clopper--Pearson upper bounds below $10^{-5}$ for both conditions under the binomial model. The interface supports address-tracked injection, transversal CNOT and logical Bell-measurement constructions, and logical SWAP and Hadamard constructions with tracked code permutations. Given advance resource preparation and sufficient routing parallelism, increasing the concatenation level expands parallel encoded-resource width without increasing the protected online sequence length of these constructions. These results identify a modular route to lower logical error rates while retaining a common Gaussian MBQC operation set with shallow online processing.

infographic.key_insight: A factory–processor interface separates verified, code-dependent optical resource preparation from reusable Gaussian processing for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: With advance resource preparation and sufficient routing parallelism, deeper error-correcting codes increase parallel resource width without lengthening the protected online sequences of the demonstrated constructions.
method: Prepare verified logical Bell resources offline using recursively concatenated C4 codes built from physical GKP qubits.
Inject resources into a time-domain measurement-based processor through an interface tracking mode mappings, measurements, frames, and verification records.
Construct logical CNOT, Bell measurement, SWAP, and Hadamard operations with address and code-permutation tracking.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations at 12.25 dB support decreasing logical Bell errors from concatenation levels 2 through 5; a separate fixed-sample evaluation at 15.6 dB and level 2 gives one-sided 95% binomial upper bounds below 10⁻⁵, both with and without prescribed post-injection noise.
infographic.watch_item: The reported gains depend on the specified displacement-noise model and fixed postselection policy; practical scaling also requires sufficient routing parallelism and advance resource availability.
infographic.paper_title: Modular optical fault-tolerant quantum computation via an interface between verified resources and online logical operations

title: Trident: Efficient Load Verification for Yoked Surface Codes using a Three-Level Memory Hierarchy
authors: Gunagya Singh Mamak, Suhas Vittal, Kabir Dubey, Kaitlin N. Smith, Moinuddin K. Qureshi
abstract: Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers (FTQCs) commonly use the surface code to encode program qubits as error-corrected logical qubits. Unfortunately, the surface code has a poor encoding rate, so recent work has proposed Yoked Surface Codes (YSCs), which concatenate the surface code with a high-rate quantum code. The surface code qubits in YSCs are protected by the checks, or yokes, of the high-rate code. YSCs have 1D and 2D variants, which are $1.8\times$ and $4.5\times$ more efficient than the surface code, respectively. Modern FTQC architectures use a two-level hierarchy: surface codes perform logical operations (compute) while 2D YSCs store idle program qubits (memory). To load a qubit from memory, the FTQC first performs retrieval, which logically moves a program qubit from a 2D YSC into a surface code (8 cycles). However, retrieval is not fault-tolerant, so the FTQC must verify the load by measuring all the yokes of the 2D YSC (178 cycles). As verification dominates memory access latency, eliminating it can provide a speedup of $5.7\times$. Our goal is to reduce the verification overhead of 2D YSCs while retaining their storage efficiency. We exploit the fact that 1D YSCs, though less storage-efficient, incur negligible verification latency. We propose Trident, which expands the two-level hierarchy into a three-level hierarchy by adding a small intermediate level containing a 1D YSC (L1). If most loads hit L1 rather than L2 (2D YSC tier), it can significantly reduce verification overhead. We present two variants: Trident-D (demand-driven) and Trident-P (prefetch-driven), which achieve speedups of $2.8\times$ and $4.2\times$, respectively, while increasing the physical qubit cost of memory by only 4.9%.

infographic.key_insight: Trident adds a small 1D yoked surface code tier between compute and dense quantum memory to reduce costly load verification.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A three-level memory hierarchy can accelerate fault-tolerant quantum computing while largely preserving the storage efficiency of 2D yoked surface codes.
method: Use surface codes for compute, 1D yoked surface codes for L1, and dense 2D yoked surface codes for L2.
Serve most loads from L1, where verification latency is negligible, avoiding expensive L2 verification.
Manage L1 with demand-driven Trident-D or prefetch-driven Trident-P.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 2.8× speedup for Trident-D and 4.2× for Trident-P, with only a 4.9% increase in memory physical-qubit cost.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits depend on serving most loads from the small L1 tier; workload locality and prefetch effectiveness are key implementation concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Trident: Efficient Load Verification for Yoked Surface Codes using a Three-Level Memory Hierarchy

title: Graphical Rigidity of Continuous Variable Graph States under Gaussian Local Transformations
authors: Giorgio Ciliberto, Frédéric Grosshans
abstract: Multimode entangled pure Gaussian states are an essential resource for continuous variable (CV) quantum information processing. Menicucci et al. [2011] have shown how to describe them as graphs with complex adjacency matrices. Among such complex graph states (CGSs), quantum optics experimental setups straightforwardly display correlations described by purely imaginary graph states (iRGSs) whereas theoretical literature favors off-diagonal real graph state (RGS) descriptions, which actually reflect the entanglement structure in the infinite squeezing limit [Gonzalez-Arciniegas et al. 2021]. We study them beyond this ideal case, thus establishing in the finite squeezing regime an equivalence criterion for the generic case of CGSs through a graph propagating set of conditions which either finds a Gaussian Local Unitary (GLU) converting one state to another or gives a proof of impossibility if such a GLU does not exist. In the experimentally relevant case of the conversion between iRGSs and RGSs, the set of conditions results in simple relations between the topologies of the equivalent real and imaginary graphs. Finally, we show that the canonical forms of iRGSs and RGSs imply that the topology of the CV real and imaginary graph states are too rigid to admit any exact qumode local-addition analogue to the qubit complementation or qudit local-addition, thus demonstrating the non-existence of any exact qumode local-addition for these states. We however define an approximate one when the squeezing is strong enough.

infographic.key_insight: At finite squeezing, continuous-variable graph states obey topology constraints that rule out exact qumode local-addition analogues of qubit local complementation or qudit local addition.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The equivalence criterion can help determine whether experimentally accessible imaginary graph states can be converted into desired real graph states using Gaussian local unitaries.
method: Propagate graph-based conditions to construct a Gaussian local conversion or prove its impossibility.
Derive topology relations for equivalent real and purely imaginary graph states.
Use canonical forms to establish rigidity and define approximate local addition at sufficiently strong squeezing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical equivalence criteria and impossibility results, with no experimental data or numerical benchmarks described.
infographic.watch_item: Approximate local addition requires sufficiently strong squeezing; the abstract provides no quantitative squeezing threshold or approximation-error bound.
infographic.paper_title: Graphical Rigidity of Continuous Variable Graph States under Gaussian Local Transformations

title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation
authors: Ouns El Harzli, Jelle Bor, Linde Wester, Leonid Zhukov, Hanl Park, Jean-François Bobier
abstract: We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observables can be obtained using a diagrammatic GW-based embedding, either GW+DMFT or self-energy embedding theory (SEET), applied to a DFT-screened shortlist. The atomistic electrode/electrolyte interface defines the electronic structure problem from which the correlated impurity models are constructed. Quantum impurity solvers would provide the finite-temperature impurity Green's functions required by the embedding. The computational challenges that classical solvers may encounter as the interacting active space grows, together with the polynomial scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation for efficiently represented discretized models, open an opportunity for quantum advantage. We identify the benchmarks needed to assess this opportunity through convergence of vacancy and migration energetics and comparison with the best applicable classical solvers. We provide illustrative logical qubit counts and identify the thermal state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs needed for a complete resource assessment. We connect microscopic observables to macroscopic engineering metrics using a continuum model for mixed ionic--electronic conducting oxygen electrodes that couples oxygen surface exchange, solid-state oxygen transport, electrode microstructure, and finite electrode thickness. Finally, we estimate the potential worldwide business value of improved electrode materials under SOFC and SOEC deployment scenarios informed by public technical targets and electrolyser deployment data.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum impurity solvers could help screen strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials, but quantum advantage remains to be demonstrated.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework links atomic-scale electrode properties to solid oxide fuel cell and electrolyser performance, enabling assessment of potential engineering and business value.
method: Use DFT screening to shortlist materials and construct correlated impurity models from electrode–electrolyte interfaces.
Combine GW+DMFT or SEET embedding with quantum-computed finite-temperature impurity Green’s functions.
Connect vacancy energetics and electronic conductivity to continuum electrode models and deployment scenarios.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports illustrative logical-qubit counts and scenario-based value estimates, while specifying convergence tests and classical-solver comparisons needed to assess quantum advantage.
infographic.watch_item: A complete resource assessment must include thermal-state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated impurity solves—not just logical-qubit counts.
infographic.paper_title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation
